 California Proposition Roundup: What Passed and What Failed
 Voters weighed in on 14 state propositions; seven will become law, and seven others lost. Nov 20, 2026 Updated 1:52 pm PT Tyche Hendricks 
 A polling place at Hoogasian Flowers in San Francisco on Nov. 3, 2026.  (Beth LaBerge/KQED) California voters decided the outcome of 14 state propositions this fall, including measures to tax the wealth of billionaires, require voters to show ID, speed up environmental reviews and fund affordable housing, schools and healthcare.
 With more than 99% of all votes tallied statewide on Friday — representing 13.4 million voters, two and a half weeks after Election Day — seven measures had earned enough support to be declared winners by the Associated Press, while another six definitely failed. One final measure was trailing and supporters conceded the race.
 What passed
 Proposition 1: Housing bond 
 Voters approved this bond measure that will authorize the state to borrow $10 billion to fund affordable housing and related infrastructure projects and another $1.25 billion for a home loan program for veterans.
 According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office , the funds will support up to 40,000 rental units and will also assist 40,000 families in buying a home.
 Construction crews work at the site of RISE, an affordable housing development, across the street from the Berryessa/North San Jose BART Station, in San Jose on July 16, 2026.  (Gina Castro for KQED) 
 At a time when the cost of housing is a critical concern for many California families, this measure, put on the ballot by state lawmakers, reflects a big investment in tackling the problem.
 “There’s really only so much bond debt we can take on as a state, so we want to be mindful,” said East Bay Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, who worked for years to get the housing bond on the ballot. “This year, the housing bond really became the priority because we’re running out of these resources.”
 Proposition 2: Rainy day fund 
 This measure to shore up California’s “rainy day fund,” formally known as the Budget Stabilization Account, sailed to victory on election night.
 California has a progressive tax structure, meaning high earners pay a higher rate. That tends to produce big fluctuations in revenue from year to year, depending on how the economy — and the stock market — are doing.
 Proposition 2 will build on the efforts by Gov. Jerry Brown a dozen years ago to stash away some tax dollars during good years as a buffer for lean times.
 The measure will expand the fund’s maximum size from 10% of general fund tax revenue to 20%. It also exempts deposits into the rainy day fund from counting against the state spending limit — and allows money that’s set aside for paying state debts to cover more types of loans.
 Proposition 3: Income taxes 
 California voters approved this measure to make permanent a tax on high earners that is set to expire in 2031.
 In 2012, voters increased tax rates for the top 2% of earners (and extended the increase in 2016) — generating roughly $10 billion a year for the general fund.
 Students arrive at Jose Ortega Elementary School for the first day of their school year on August 17, 2026, in San Francisco.  (Miles Cull/KQED) 
 The big winners of these taxes are public schools and safety net healthcare, which get the lion’s share of general fund spending.
 Under this state tax, individuals pay a marginal tax rate of a little over 10% on income above $371,000, and couples pay that on income over $743,000. 
 Higher rates of just over 11% and 12% apply further up the income ladder to couples making more than $1.5 million.
 Prop 5: Recall rules 
 A measure to change California’s system for recall elections has passed. 
 Under existing law, when a state official faces a recall, voters are asked two questions: Should the official be removed from office? And who should replace them? Proposition 5 will eliminate the second question and, if the person is recalled, the governor would appoint a replacement or (for legislative vacancies) there would be a special election.
Proponents say that should eliminate a situation where a successor can win without a majority vote.
 Proposition 37: Homebuyer bond 
 Proposition 37, a measure meant to ease the crisis over housing costs in California, won handily on election night.
 The $25 billion bond measure will enable the state to create a down-payment assistance loan program for would-be homeowners earning up to 200% of an area’s median income.
 Close-up of a “for sale” sign on post in front yard of house  (Grace Cary/Getty Images) 
 The measure, which was placed on the ballot by a coalition of real estate interests and building trades unions, will only apply to newly constructed homes.
 Proposition 38: Immunology bond 
 Voters also passed another bond measure, focused on immunotherapy research. The $8.4 billion bond measure generated controversy over the fact that half the money would go to an untested institute at UCLA backed by the same billionaire who paid to get Proposition 38 on the ballot. 
 Opponents said priorities for public spending on medical research should be based on rigorous scientific review and public health needs. Supporters said that at a time when federal funding is unreliable, California should take the lead in supporting cutting edge research.
 The UCLA campus in Los Angeles on Feb. 18, 2022.  (Raquel Natalicchio for CalMatters) 
 Prop 42: Tax limits 
 Proposition 42 won by a narrow margin. It was placed on the ballot by opponents of the billionaire wealth tax, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin.
 The measure will make it much harder to pass future wealth taxes, by prohibiting new levies on the ownership of financial assets, such as stocks and personal property, that are typically only taxed when they generate income or are sold.
 What failed
 Prop 4: Campaign financing 
 More than two weeks after the election, with Proposition 4 trailing by a narrow but steady margin, supporters conceded the race.
 The measure would have allowed any state or local government to set up a public financing program for election campaigns. It would have repealed a 1988 ban on using taxpayer dollars for election campaigns. Currently, only charter cities and counties can bypass that ban.
 Under the measure, candidates would have needed to meet certain eligibility criteria and agree to spending limits and other restrictions on the use of the funds.
 Proposition 39: Voter ID 
 Voters soundly defeated Proposition 39, a measure that would have required Californians to show ID when voting.
 Under current law, when Californians register to vote, they must provide an ID number — and their signature swearing they are eligible adult citizens.
 They don’t need to show ID when they vote, but they must sign in at the polls or sign their ballot envelope, and that signature is matched with the original on their registration form.
 Sen. Tony Strickland speaks at the Riverside County Registrar of Voters on March 2, 2026, for a press conference highlighting voter signatures in favor of placing a voter ID measure on the November ballot.  (Anjali Sharif-Paul/MediaNews Group/The Sun via Getty Images) 
 Proposition 39 would have required voters to present ID at the polls (or an ID number when voting by mail).
 Opponents argued the system already works, and Proposition 39 was a solution in search of a problem that could disenfranchise some eligible voters.
 Proposition 40: Billionaire wealth tax 
 This wealth tax measure, aimed at funding safety net health services, drew some of the greatest debate — and money — of any California proposition this year. On Monday night, the AP called it a defeat.
 The measure was placed on the state ballot by a union of health care workers, at a time when Congress has made deep cuts to Medicaid (known in California as Medi-Cal).
 A supporter with the Billionaire Tax Now coalition holds a placard during a media briefing in Los Angeles on April 27, 2026.  (Frederic J. Brown/AFP via Getty Images) 
 The measure would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of individuals whose assets are valued at over $1 billion. 
 The “No” campaign was bankrolled with over $160 million from a group of tech billionaires who stood to be taxed.
 Proposition 41: Tax audits 
 Propositions 41 and 42 were placed on the ballot by the same tech leaders who opposed the billionaire wealth tax, and either would have nullified Proposition 40 if it passed with more votes. Proposition 41 failed to pass, while Proposition 42 was leading in a race that the AP has yet to call. 
 Proposition 41 would have required ongoing audits of state programs that are funded by “special” taxes earmarked for a specific purpose, to assess whether they are spending money wisely. 
 Proposition 43: Local taxes 
 Proposition 43, a measure that would have made it harder to pass new local tax measures, failed.
 Live 2026 Election Results Learn about the results of the California Propositions The measure — supported by Republicans and anti-tax groups and opposed by Democrats, unions and California counties — would have required a two-thirds vote, rather than a simple majority, to pass any local taxes earmarked for a specific purpose, such as schools or wildfire prevention.
California voters approved the two-thirds majority threshold in 1996, but in 2017 the state Supreme Court ruled that it only applied to measures put on the ballot by elected officials. 
 Proposition 43 would have applied it to voter initiatives as well. 
 Proposition 44: Health clinics 
 A measure to require nonprofit community health clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue on patient services was overwhelmingly defeated on election night, with four out of five voters rejecting it.
The same healthcare workers union behind Proposition 40 put this measure on the ballot, saying it was important to ensure taxpayer dollars are not spent on excessive salaries and overhead.
 The state Legislative Analyst’s Office has found that community clinics currently spend about 80% of revenue on services. 
 Opponents — including clinics and physician groups — say the sector is already heavily regulated and the measure would have harmed community care by adding red tape.
 Proposition 45: CEQA review 
 Voters rejected Proposition 45, a measure that would reshape the state’s landmark environmental law, the California Environmental Quality Act, to expedite certain projects deemed “essential.” 
 The 1970 law requires agencies to consider environmental harm before building, but developers say it’s often used to delay important affordable housing and infrastructure projects. 
 Proposition 45 would have set a one-year time limit on environmental reviews, and a 270-day limit for courts to rule on related lawsuits. Opponents pointed out it was financed by utilities and corporate PACs, and said it could gut environmental protections.
 This story includes reporting from KQED staff and our partner CalMatters.
